extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning elementary kinematics/geometry of motion (advanced-secondary/undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance for representing point-motion by geometrical diagrams: how to construct and read time-charts (distance vs time), maps of path, velocity-diagrams (hodographs), and curvature/acceleration charts to measure speed, velocity, acceleration, and curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical time-chart (time-chart) construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Place stations (or positions along the path) on a vertical distance-axis and times on a horizontal time-axis, scaling so that fixed fractions of an inch represent given distance units (e.g., furlongs/miles) and minutes respectively; connect corresponding station and time coordinates to obtain points Q1, Q2, ... and join them by a continuous line to form the time-chart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale choices allow direct reading of distance for any time or time for any position. Example procedure: plot station positions vertically, plot travel times horizontally (e.g., 1/8 in = 1 minute), draw horizontal through a station and vertical through its time to get a point on the chart; join points to form the curve. The time-chart may contain small horizontal pieces at stops; more densely sampled positions approximate a continuous curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-chart + map fully describes point-motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination of the time-chart and a map of the path fully describes a point-motion: the time-chart gives exact times for every position and the map gives the directions (bearings) and sense of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using both figures together you can determine (a) the exact time the train takes to reach any point along the path and (b) the exact position at any given time (example: find how far the train has gone in 26 minutes by scaling on the time-axis, drawing vertical to the curve, then horizontal to the distance-axis). Authors call as a fundamental problem: to ascertain the map and the time-chart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slope as measure of steepness (straight lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a straight sloping line AC, the slope is the ratio of vertical rise to horizontal run (units risen per unit horizontal distance) and is a fitting measure of steepness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if AB = 100 ft and CB (vertical) = 20 ft then slope = 20/100 = 1/5; equivalently expressable in different proportional units (2 ft in 10 ft, etc.). Slope is the number of units risen vertically per one horizontal unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean slope and tangent slope for curves
rubrics_metrics.description: The slope of a chord AC of a curve is the mean slope of that portion of the curve; the tangent is the limiting position of the chord as the chord endpoint approaches the point A and its slope measures the steepness of the curve at A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret chord slope as the average steepness between two points. Use the limiting process (imagine a bent wire and a straight wire sliding into tangent position) to define the tangent and thus the instantaneous slope; note this limit cannot be attained in direct perception but is a key descriptive conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed as slope: average and instantaneous
rubrics_metrics.description: On the time-chart the slope of a chord equals the mean (average) speed over the corresponding time interval; the slope of the tangent (limit of the chord) is the actual (instantaneous) speed at that instant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret slope numerically as space units per time unit (e.g., miles per minute). Shorter chords give mean speeds over smaller intervals, approaching instantaneous speed. If the time-chart is a straight line the speed is uniform; otherwise speed is variable. Varying the scales changes interpretation of the same geometric slope into units of miles per minute, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity as combination of speed and bearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocity combines speed (the numerical magnitude measured by the slope of the tangent on the time-chart) and bearing (the direction of the tangent on the path map together with its sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent velocity by a step (vector): magnitude of the step measures speed, direction of the step shows direction of motion, and an arrow-head gives the sense. To fully describe velocity at a point you must specify both magnitude and bearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity diagram / hodograph construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the hodograph by drawing from a pole I a series of rays parallel to the tangents at successive path points P1, P2, ... and measuring off along these rays lengths equal to the speed at those points; the endpoints form a curve (the hodograph) whose rays measure the velocities of P relative to the pole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each ray from the pole is a step representing the velocity at the corresponding point of the path. With many sample points the velocity-points approach a curve (the hodograph). The hodograph visually describes how the motion is changing in both magnitude and direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration as velocity of a point on the hodograph
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceleration of the original motion is represented by the velocity of the point V as it moves along the hodograph (i.e., the rate of change of the velocity-vector).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the hodograph as the map of a new motion: the velocity of V along its curve measures the change in the velocity of P. One may draw a second hodograph (hodograph of the hodograph) to obtain a diagram of accelerations; in general acceleration stands in the same relation to velocity as velocity to position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration decomposed into spurt and shunt
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceleration has two fundamental factors: (i) spurt — change in speed (stretching of the velocity-step IV), and (ii) shunt — change in bearing (spin of IV about the pole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when a train speeds up from 40 to 60 mph and alters bearing from north to north-east, it is spurted and shunted. Mean spurt = increase of speed per unit time (Δlength/Δt). Mean shunt (or mean spin) = increase of angle per unit time (Δangle/Δt). Mean acceleration = combined rate of spurting and shunting over the interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration via vector addition (step V4V5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change from an old velocity IV4 to a new velocity IV5 can be represented by adding the small step V4V5 to IV4 (parallelogram law); the mean acceleration is expressed by the step V4V5 divided by the time interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two equivalent constructive views: (a) stretch IV4 to IV5 (spurt) then spin to direction IV5 (shunt), or (b) add the small step V4V5 geometrically to IV4. In the limit of small intervals both methods yield the same actual acceleration (velocity of V along the hodograph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration represented and measured as a step
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual acceleration may be represented by a step whose bearing denotes the direction and sense in which the velocity-vector is changing and whose length denotes the number of units of speed added per unit time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand increments of velocity to be added geometrically by the parallelogram law (e.g., IV5 = IV4 + V4V5). The small step V4V5 (possibly infinitesimal) expresses instantaneous acceleration in the given direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature: mean and actual curvature (bending measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean curvature over a curve element P4P5 is defined as the ratio of the angle through which the tangent turns (L4NL5) to the length of that curve element (P4P5); actual curvature at a point is the limit of the mean curvature as the element length tends to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a curvature-chart analogous to the time-chart: plot successive tangent-angle increments horizontally and arc lengths vertically; the slope of a chord on this chart measures mean curvature, and the slope of the tangent to the curvature-chart at the corresponding point gives the actual curvature. For a circle mean curvature equals 1/radius; actual curvature is the inverse of the radius of curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between curvature, spin, speed and normal acceleration
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the spin (rate of turning of the tangent, angle per unit time) to the speed of the point equals the actual curvature at that position; acceleration due purely to change of direction (with constant speed) is normal (at right angles) to the velocity and corresponds to motion of V on a circular hodograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From P4 to P5 with constant speed IV4, arc length = speed × time; spin S = angle turned / time; mean curvature = S / IV4. In the limit this connects kinematics (spin and speed) to geometry (curvature). When IV is not stretched (no spurt) the hodograph is circular and acceleration is purely shunt (normal acceleration).
